extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, media researchers, broadcasters, and media policymakers interested in impartiality and sourcing practices
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how impartiality and balance are operationalised in news output (particularly BBC radio, television and online), using sourcing patterns, source diversity, prominence and policy-practice comparisons. The page reports a quantitative content-analysis approach and discusses implications for editorial policy and journalistic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality — breadth and diversity of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Impartiality entails provision of a broad view of the range and weight of opinion on a particular topic; journalists should take account of (i) a full range of views and opinions; (ii) the relative weight of opinion; and (iii) changes that occur in the range and weight of opinion over time (Hartley, 1992). The BBC editorial guidelines commit to reflecting a breadth and diversity of opinion across output over an appropriate period so that no significant strand is knowingly unreflected or under-represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires curatorial judgement given time/space constraints; assess breadth across output and over appropriate time periods rather than single items; differentiate across genres and domestic/international content; treat breadth as both numeric diversity of sources and substantive diversity of views/weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance (seesaw) — equal space to opposing views
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance understood as allocation of equal space to opposing views (the 'seesaw' metaphor) — juxtaposing two poles (typically the two main political parties) to avoid appearance of bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should be aware this operationalisation can oversimplify the political spectrum, privilege partisan conflict over substantive context, and fail when there are more than two meaningful positions or when a consensus exists (e.g., scientific issues). Use caution when equating equal time with impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wagon wheel model — many spokes of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bridcut Review's 'wagon wheel' model: impartiality requires greater subtlety in covering and counterpointing the varied shades of opinion — more than just two sides of an argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure presence of multiple distinct viewpoints (beyond binary opposites) and the representation of nuanced shades of opinion; consider whether editorial policy changes (e.g. adopting wagon wheel) actually translate to source practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominance of elite/political sources
rubrics_metrics.description: An operational criterion: the extent to which known elites (politicians, ministers, MPs, officials) dominate source appearances. The study found political sources accounted for ~49.4% (2007) and 54.8% (2012) of sources, demonstrating elite dominance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High share of elite sources signals narrowing of views and potential failure of impartiality-as-breadth; assess whether elites are 'primary definers' and whether non-elite voices are marginalized or relegated to reactive roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political party balance and partisan representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the partisan composition of political sources (e.g., Conservative, Labour, Lib Dem, SNP) and whether particular parties or viewpoints are over- or under-represented (the study shows Conservative over-representation in many samples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure counts/percentages of party-affiliated sources, consider political context and media personas (e.g., incumbency or leader charisma), and evaluate whether apparent imbalance reflects editorial choices or news-event-driven prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source diversity (types and number of sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the variety of source types used in coverage (political sources; members of the public; media/journalists; public sector; religious leaders; NGOs/activists; academics; judiciary; think tanks; business, etc.) and the number of different sources per story (the study coded up to 16 sources per story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding should capture both counts and types; remember that numerical diversity of sources may not equal diversity of viewpoints. Compare across stories/platforms and examine whether non-elite professions are given substantive space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source prominence and ordering within stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess where source types appear within a story (e.g., political sources disproportionately feature among the first eight sources, framing the report, while members of the public tend to appear later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the placement of sources (opening sections vs later parts) because early sources strongly shape framing; compare distribution across first vs later sources to evaluate agenda-setting power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration and prominence of source contributions (soundbite length / word count)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the duration of direct quotations in broadcasts and word counts for online content as indicators of how much space and weight each source is given (the study coded soundbite lengths and online word counts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short soundbites (e.g., 1–10 seconds) often characterize members of the public, whereas political/authoritative sources receive longer segments (11–20 seconds+). Use durations/word counts to assess substantive influence, not just appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform and programme differences in breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how different platforms and programme formats (flagship TV/radio shows vs online stories vs audience-participation programmes) vary in their inclusion of diverse voices; the study found online coverage had the largest number of stories and was more likely to include broader ranges of opinion, while flagship programmes were less likely to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare across platforms and programme types; account for format constraints (time limits, programme length) and affordances (online capacity) when judging breadth of opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial policy vs newsroom practice (policy implementation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether top-down editorial statements or reviews (e.g., Bridcut Review, BBC editorial guidelines) are implemented in day-to-day sourcing practices and whether paradigms of practice persist despite policy changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use longitudinal or before/after comparisons (e.g., 2007 vs 2012) and examine routine newsroom practices that sustain paradigms (deadline pressures, indexing to party-political conflicts) to evaluate effectiveness of policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content analysis methodological standards (coding, piloting, intercoder reliability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for research evaluating sourcing: develop a coding scheme, pilot extensively, use trained coders, and test intercoder reliability (the study reports piloting and >80% agreement on reliability tests).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report unit of analysis, source caps (e.g., up to 16 sources), piloting process, intercoder reliability measures and thresholds, and any excluded variables due to low reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and timeframe considerations (representativeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that samples provide 'snapshots' and are limited by selection of programmes, platforms, and timeframes; avoid major events that could skew results, but note that some news events will shape prominence of topics/sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose sampling windows carefully, justify selection, report limitations, and interpret findings as indicative of patterns within the sampled period rather than definitive statements about all output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic representativeness of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess sources by demographic variables (gender, age, ethnicity, religion, region) to evaluate whether coverage reflects societal diversity; the study coded these variables though not all were reported due to space and some were excluded when reliability was low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include demographic coding in analyses, report any variables excluded for reliability reasons, and use demographic measures alongside source-type and viewpoint analyses to assess inclusive representation.
